title: Chrome adopts what may be the best protection yet against account takeovers
gist: Chrome has shipped device-bound session credentials (DBSCs) in version 147 on Windows and 150 on macOS, binding session cookies to a private key sealed in the TPM or secure enclave so stolen cookies cannot be replayed. This directly counters the infostealer and adversary-in-the-middle attacks that emerged as attackers routed around 2FA and passkeys, and extends the no-shared-secret authentication model from login to the whole session.

themes.theme: Session cookie theft as the post-2FA attack path

insights.claim: Session cookie theft has grown as a primary account-takeover vector precisely because 2FA and passkeys made password phishing ineffective, pushing attackers toward infostealer malware and adversary-in-the-middle attacks that grab the post-login session instead.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Security hardening displaces attacks rather than eliminating them — the infostealer economy is the direct downstream consequence of MFA adoption, and it is where defensive spending must follow.
insights.quote: Once possession of a mere password is no longer sufficient, phishing and other more traditional forms of account takeovers are no longer effective.
insights.locator: An antidote to session cookie theft

insights.claim: Stolen session cookies work because an attacker can paste them into their own browser and obtain the same access as the legitimate owner, bypassing every authentication factor that was checked at login.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Login-time authentication strength is irrelevant to session-replay attacks — a reason MFA rollout metrics overstate real account-takeover protection.
insights.quote: Attackers then paste the cookies into their own browser and gain the same access the rightful owner has (at least temporarily).
insights.locator: To compensate, attackers have increasingly relied on infostealer malware

insights.claim: Chrome's device-bound session credentials store a unique encryption key in the machine's TPM on Windows or secure enclave on macOS and iOS, and require the browser to send each session cookie signed with that non-extractable key.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Hardware key storage becomes load-bearing for ordinary web sessions, not just login — raising the practical value of TPM/secure-enclave silicon across the installed base.
insights.locator: The new Chrome protection is known as device-bound session credentials

insights.claim: Report URI founder Scott Helme frames the core protection as key non-extractability: an attacker can still steal the cookie but cannot answer a DBSC challenge because the TPM or Secure Enclave will not release the private key.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The defense assumes hardware key isolation holds, making TPM/enclave integrity the single point of failure for the entire session-security model.
insights.quote: The attacker can steal the cookie, but they can’t answer a DBSC challenge by signing it with the private key, which is still safe on your device.
insights.locator: “The attacker can’t steal the private key from the device

insights.claim: DBSC extends the no-shared-secret model to sessions: web servers store the visitor's public key and issue an authentication challenge incorporating the session cookie, rejecting any assertion not signed by the device-held private key — the same mechanism passkeys use for login.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The industry is converging on asymmetric-key challenge-response across the whole authenticated lifecycle, which progressively strands vendors whose products depend on interceptable shared secrets.
insights.quote: DBSCs are the latest form of authentication that eliminates the reliance on a shared secret, which, as the world has known for years, is painfully easy for attackers to steal.
insights.locator: DBSCs are the latest form of authentication

insights.claim: DBSCs are currently supported only in Chrome version 147 for Windows and version 150 for macOS, and even there are enabled for only a limited set of users, indicating Google is still testing before general availability.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Real-world protection is negligible today — do not credit DBSC in near-term breach-risk models until general availability lands.
insights.quote: For the moment, DBSCs are supported only in Chrome version 147 for Windows and 150 for macOS. Even then, DBSCs are turned on only for a limited set of users.
insights.locator: For the moment, DBSCs are supported only in Chrome

insights.claim: Protection requires server-side support as well as browser support, since 'device bound sessions' only appears in Chrome developer tools when a user is logged into a site that implements DBSCs.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Adoption is a two-sided coordination problem — relying-party implementation, not browser shipping, is the rate limiter on when infostealer losses actually fall.
insights.locator: Chrome users on Windows and macOS can check whether it’s running

insights.claim: It is unclear when or whether other Chromium-based browsers will implement DBSCs, though the author judges it likely they will follow.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Google is again setting a de facto web security standard through Chrome distribution power, a dynamic that shapes both the security roadmap and antitrust attention.
insights.quote: It’s unclear when, or if, other Chromium-based browsers will implement DBSCs, but it’s likely they will be coming.
insights.locator: It’s unclear when, or if, other Chromium-based browsers
